addressed_problems.content: Although the empirical results demonstrate a strong correlation between the ℓ2 learning distance from initialization and the three-phase sparse double descent curve—where staying close to initialization coincides with better robustness in the Sweet Phase and moving far leads to overfitting in the Critical Phase—a rigorous theoretical account proving or falsifying this hypothesis is lacking. A principled derivation linking ℓ2 distance from initialization to memorization propensity and to the observed double descent behavior in sparse neural networks remains an open problem, whose resolution would provide a mechanistic understanding of why sparsity can both aggravate and relieve overfitting.

The predictive power of the ℓ2 learning distance as a generalization measure for sparse models is confounded by scale invariances inherent in rectified neural networks, such as ReLU rescaling and batch normalization reparametrizations. These invariances can inflate or deflate the measured distance without altering network behavior, as observed in the CIFAR experiments where the learning distance curve did not exhibit a distinct peak in the Critical Phase unlike the MNIST results. The precise role of these invariances in modulating learning distance and the development of a scale-invariant diagnostic that retains predictive power for sparse double descent remain unresolved issues.

Empirically, the location and width of the Critical Phase and Sweet Phase in the sparse double descent phenomenon depend on dataset difficulty, label-noise rate, architecture, and training schedule—for instance, increasing label noise shifts the Critical Phase to lower sparsities and the Sweet Phase to higher sparsities. However, the mechanisms that determine these transitions are not characterized theoretically. Understanding how these factors influence the interpolation threshold and the beneficial regularization regime is necessary to predict when pruning will hurt or help generalization.

The paper shows that different retraining strategies—lottery ticket rewinding, finetuning, learning rate rewinding, and scratch reinitialization—yield markedly different performance at the same sparsity level, with randomly reinitialized models sometimes outperforming lottery ticket models. Yet the theoretical reasons why certain strategies excel at particular sparsities remain unexplained. A theory linking retraining initialization, optimization dynamics, and the phase structure of sparse double descent is needed to guide the choice of retraining method.

Beyond individual gaps, the paper leaves open the development of a unified theoretical framework that connects the reshaping of the loss landscape induced by sparsity—including the creation of spurious minima and valleys reported in prior theoretical work—with optimization dynamics under sparsity constraints and generalization in noisy-label regimes. Such a framework would integrate the empirical observations of sparse double descent, the learning distance correlation, and the failure of minima flatness into a coherent theory of how pruning affects the learning behavior of deep networks.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are typically trained with far more parameters than training examples, which produces extreme overparameterization that both enables powerful function approximation and creates a large capacity to memorize training data. Prior work has studied how increasing model capacity can produce a "deep double descent" in test performance as a function of capacity, and a large body of pruning research treats parameter removal as a way to reduce capacity and thus to regularize models. In practice, pruning is widely applied using heuristics (e.g., magnitude-based, gradient-based, or random unstructured pruning) and is commonly believed to either preserve or improve generalization by restricting redundant parameters, by injecting noise, or by encouraging flatter minima. However, there is no settled understanding of how progressively increasing sparsity (model parameter removal) changes generalization, especially in regimes where overfitting is severe (for example, when training labels are corrupted). Because prior work has not systematically characterized generalization as a function of model sparsity across architectures, datasets, pruning heuristics and retraining procedures, researchers lack principled guidance about when pruning will help versus hurt: which sparsity ranges reduce memorization of noisy labels, which ranges cause worse overfitting despite reduced parameter counts, and how to interpret these effects with existing measures (e.g., minima flatness). The absence of this characterization prevents reliable prediction and control of pruning effects on generalization, limits theoretical understanding of sparsity-induced optimization and generalization phenomena, and leaves open whether pruning-era concepts such as the lottery ticket hypothesis hold uniformly across sparsity regimes and noisy-label settings.

nodes.content: Researchers have commonly assumed that pruning monotonically reduces model capacity and thus reduces overfitting, so pruning is often used to improve efficiency and sometimes thought to regularize models. Prior empirical studies of pruning report that many heuristics preserve accuracy and sometimes limit memorization, but they have not reported a general, systematic three-stage test-accuracy vs. sparsity curve. Without an established empirical characterization, practitioners cannot know whether pruning at a given sparsity will improve or worsen test performance, particularly under label corruption. The absence of such a cross-architecture, cross-dataset empirical law prevents principled choices of pruning degree in noisy or overfitting-prone settings and leaves open whether phenomena analogous to deep double descent occur under model sparsification.

Observing non-monotonic test behavior as sparsity increases requires a language to localize where pruning helps or hurts. Prior literature typically reports coarse accuracy-vs-sparsity curves without resolving narrow regimes near interpolation thresholds, and lacks a concise phase description that explains why moderate pruning sometimes increases overfitting while heavier pruning later relieves it. Without such a decomposition into regimes, analysis of pruning effects, comparisons across methods, and targeted interventions (e.g., choosing retraining strategy or sparsity target) remain ad hoc and poorly informed.

The prevailing expectation is that reducing parameters should reduce memorization capacity; hence pruning is often applied to combat overfitting. However, instances where moderate pruning increases the generalization gap contradict this expectation. Prior empirical reports that pruning impairs memorization did not reveal this nuanced behavior in which pruning hurts generalization while preserving train accuracy, and theory lacks an account of why parameter removal can temporarily increase a model's tendency to overfit noisy labels. Consequently, practitioners have no clear warning that commonly used intermediate sparsities may harm test-time performance even when train loss is unaffected.

A common explanatory hypothesis for generalization after pruning is that pruning encourages flatter minima, and flatness correlates with better generalization. If pruning-induced flatness explained performance, then reintroducing pruned parameters with small learning rates should keep solutions near the original (flat) basin. Prior work invoked flatness as a regularizer but did not test whether sparse solutions remain minimizers in the dense parameterization. The lack of such tests means the field cannot conclude whether flatness is the operative mechanism behind pruning-related generalization effects; this uncertainty obstructs theoretical interpretations and practical advice when pruning is applied under severe overfitting conditions.

Existing generalization diagnostics (e.g., minima sharpness/flatness) fail to explain why pruning sometimes worsens and sometimes improves generalization. Meanwhile, theoretical and empirical work has suggested that distance from initialization constrains model capacity and the tendency to memorize noisy labels, but that perspective had not been systematically connected to pruning-induced non-monotonic behavior. Without an explicit, measurable quantity tied to initialization that correlates with the sparse double descent curve, researchers and practitioners lack a practical metric to anticipate whether a given sparsity will move the model toward a more memorizing or more robust regime.

The lottery ticket hypothesis posits that certain sparse subnetworks paired with their original initialization can be trained to match dense-model performance and outperform reinitialized copies. However, this claim was not examined across sparsity regimes that exhibit sparse double descent under label noise. If sparsity can move subnetworks into regimes where rewinding is suboptimal, then the universality of the lottery-ticket conclusion is restricted; practitioners cannot assume that retaining original initialization is always the best retraining strategy across all sparsities and noise levels.

Prior evaluations often report only final-epoch test accuracy and therefore may miss the fact that pruning can improve the peak test performance achievable during training. Because training-time capacity and the number of epochs interact with generalization and double descent behavior, a lack of consideration of epoch-wise best accuracy limits conclusions about whether pruning is beneficial overall; practitioners who evaluate only final checkpoints can be misled about pruning's potential benefits for early-stopping-based workflows.

Increasing model sparsity by iterative unstructured pruning produces a non-monotonic, three-stage dependence of test performance on sparsity, termed "sparse double descent": (a) as sparsity grows from zero the test performance first degrades, (b) then at higher sparsities test performance recovers and improves substantially, and (c) at extreme sparsities performance finally collapses as useful parameters are lost. This phenomenon is observed across multiple network architectures (LeNet-300-100, ResNet-18, VGG-16, ResNet-101), datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet), label-noise regimes (symmetric, asymmetric, and pairflip noise with $\epsilon$ up to 80%), pruning heuristics (magnitude-based, gradient-based, and random pruning), and retraining schemes (lottery-ticket rewinding, finetuning, learning-rate rewinding, and scratch retraining), indicating that sparse double descent is robust to these experimental choices.

metadata.narrative: A single weak point (P1) concerns untested pruning protocols (one-shot, prune-at-init, different step sizes) that could alter or eliminate the phenomenon. H1 and H2 provide strong evidence that the phenomenon is not specific to the particular heuristic or retraining method, but P1's failure mode—the gradual nature of the pruning schedule—is not directly addressed by these highlights because they test different heuristics and retraining methods, not different pruning schedules. The interaction is one of partial insulation: the highlights demonstrate robustness across the tested dimensions, but the residual risk about the iterative protocol's step size and the one-shot vs. gradual choice remains unresolved. The dominant risk concerns generalization to alternative pruning procedures. Overall, the conclusion is credible for the protocols tested but should not be unconditionally extrapolated to all pruning methods.

nodes.title: Sparse double descent is observed across multiple architectures, datasets, pruning heuristics, retraining methods, and label-noise levels

nodes.content: Four contiguous regimes of model sparsity describe distinct training and test behaviors: (I) Light Phase — low sparsity where pruned networks retain dense-model performance; (II) Critical Phase — an intermediate sparsity interval around an interpolation threshold where training accuracy remains high but test accuracy drops (overfitting is aggravated); (III) Sweet Phase — higher sparsities where test accuracy improves substantially (reduced overfitting); (IV) Collapsed Phase — extreme sparsities where both training and test accuracy fall because too few parameters remain trainable.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified; the four phases are directly extracted from the empirical accuracy-vs-sparsity curves. The derivation is a routine description of observed trends, and no specific element of the derivation rises above the field's default to constitute a highlight. The conclusion is a well-supported descriptive taxonomy within the tested regime.

nodes.title: Four contiguous sparsity regimes (Light, Critical, Sweet, Collapsed) describe distinct training and test behaviors

nodes.content: Within the Critical Phase of sparsity (the intermediate sparsity interval around an interpolation threshold where training accuracy remains high but test accuracy drops), increasing sparsity reduces test accuracy while leaving training accuracy nearly unchanged; that is, moderate pruning increases the generalization gap and aggravates overfitting rather than mitigates it. This deterioration occurs under different pruning rules (including random pruning) and retraining methods, showing that the Critical Phase is not an artifact of a particular heuristic.

metadata.narrative: P2 identifies a key unresolved risk: the test accuracy drop in the Critical Phase might be a finite-epoch artifact rather than genuine overfitting aggravation. No highlight in the paper's derivation of this conclusion specifically addresses the training-duration concern (the highlights for Conclusion 1 confirm the existence of the drop but not its permanence). Therefore, the conclusion that moderate sparsity aggravates overfitting is vulnerable to the possibility that test accuracy would recover with more epochs. The layer of uncertainty is at the mechanism attribution (overfitting vs. slow convergence) and the quantitative magnitude. The conclusion remains plausible but requires convergence verification.

nodes.title: Moderate sparsity (the Critical Phase) can aggravate overfitting: test accuracy drops while training accuracy is preserved

nodes.content: Re-dense experiments (recovering pruned weights initialized at zero and retraining with a small learning rate) and 1-D loss/linear-interpolation visualizations show that many sparse solutions are not situated in flat basins of the dense loss landscape: when pruned weights are reintroduced and trained, the optimizer often escapes from the sparse solution toward sharper minima and overfits. Therefore, the conjecture that pruning promotes flat minima which explain improved generalization cannot account for sparse double descent.

metadata.narrative: H3 provides direct geometric evidence (monotonically decreasing loss along the interpolation path) that sparse solutions are not minimizers in the full-dimensional loss landscape, conclusively refuting a flatness-based explanation. No load-bearing weak points were identified; the re-dense experiment's dependence on zero initialization is addressed by the interpolation which does not rely on optimizer dynamics. The conclusion is strongly supported.

nodes.title: Minima flatness does not explain sparse double descent; re-dense training reveals instability of sparse solutions

nodes.content: Define the $\ell_2$ learning distance $D(\mathbf{w}_{init},\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i)=\|\mathbf{w}_{init}-\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i\|_2$, where $\mathbf{w}_{init}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is the original dense model initialization and $\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ are the learned weights after the $i$-th pruning step with pruned entries set to zero. Empirically, the curve of $D$ as a function of sparsity often tracks the sparse double descent test-accuracy curve: models in the Critical Phase (the intermediate sparsity interval around an interpolation threshold where training accuracy remains high but test accuracy drops) have larger $D$ (further from initialization) and worse test performance, whereas models in the Sweet Phase (higher sparsities where test accuracy improves substantially) are closer to initialization (smaller $D$) and generalize better. These empirical correlations hold across multiple datasets and retraining protocols, suggesting that $\ell_2$ learning distance is a useful predictor of when pruning will aggravate or relieve overfitting in sparse regimes.

metadata.narrative: P3 exposes a clear counterexample on CIFAR-100 in which the learning distance fails to track the test accuracy curve. H4 provides theoretical backing that makes the hypothesis plausible but does not resolve this empirical discrepancy. The interaction is compounding: the theoretical support cannot compensate for a direct falsification on a central dataset. The conclusion's claim of correlation across multiple datasets is not supported for CIFAR-100, and the hypothesis's general applicability is questionable. The dominant risk is that the learning distance hypothesis is only valid for certain architectures/datasets (e.g., MNIST).

nodes.title: The $\ell_2$ learning distance from initialization correlates with sparse double descent and can reflect generalization better than minima flatness

nodes.content: For certain sparsities and datasets with noisy labels, retraining a pruned subnetwork from a fresh random initialization (scratch reinit) can yield higher test accuracy than retraining the same sparse subnetwork from its original dense initialization (the lottery-ticket rewinding protocol). Thus, a subnetwork that constitutes a "winning ticket" at one sparsity/setting may not always outperform a random reinitialization in sparsity regimes where test accuracy exhibits sparse double descent (the pattern of first degrading, then improving, then collapsing with increasing sparsity).

metadata.narrative: H5 provides a clean quantitative comparison with non-overlapping error bars, directly demonstrating that scratch reinitialization can outperform lottery ticket rewinding at certain sparsities. The result is robust across noise levels and datasets. No load-bearing weak points were identified. The conclusion is highly credible.

nodes.title: Retraining a pruned subnetwork from random initialization can outperform lottery-ticket rewinding at some sparsities

nodes.content: When evaluating the best test accuracy achieved at any epoch during training (rather than the final-epoch test accuracy), pruning often increases the peak test performance from the Light Phase (low sparsity where pruned networks retain dense-model performance) into the Sweet Phase (higher sparsities where test accuracy improves substantially) before performance later declines at extreme sparsities (the Collapsed Phase). Thus pruning can enlarge the attainable best validation performance (e.g., via implicit regularization affecting training dynamics), even though final-epoch test accuracy shows the sparse double descent pattern (test accuracy first degraded, then improved, then collapsed).

metadata.narrative: P4 identifies a factual inaccuracy in the paper's description: the best-accuracy curve for magnitude pruning shows a clear drop in the Critical Phase, not a slight one. However, H6 shows that the core claim—pruning (at sweet sparsities) can increase the best achievable test accuracy—is supported across three pruning heuristics. The interaction is that P4 undermines only the peripheral claim about the gentleness of the drop, not the central claim of improvement. Therefore, the conclusion's main practical implication remains credible, but the characterisation of the trend across sparsities is overstated.

nodes.title: Pruning can improve the best-achievable test accuracy before eventual collapse at extreme sparsities

nodes.content: The iterative unstructured pruning protocol removes exactly 20% of current weights per pruning operation, retrains the network after each removal using lottery-ticket rewinding (rewinding to a fixed early iteration), and increases sparsity gradually over many steps until target sparsity is reached. This experimental design does not include alternative pruning protocols such as one-shot pruning (removing all target weights in a single operation), pruning at initialization (SNIP or GraSP), or varying the fraction of weights removed per step. Therefore, the robustness of the sparse double descent curve (the three-stage non-monotonic dependence of test accuracy on model sparsity) across pruning heuristics has been tested only for magnitude-based, gradient-based, and random iterative pruning, and has not been validated for these alternative pruning protocols.

metadata.failure_mode: If sparse double descent is absent or qualitatively different under one-shot pruning or different step sizes, the conclusion that the phenomenon is a general property of sparsity in overparameterized networks collapses to a narrower claim about a specific iterative procedure. Practical guidance for practitioners who use standard one-shot pruning would be unsupported, and the theoretical interpretation of the Critical Phase and Sweet Phase as fundamental regimes of sparsity would be weakened.
metadata.weakness_reason: The 20%-per-step iterative protocol with lottery-ticket rewinding is a narrow instantiation of all possible pruning procedures. One-shot pruning is widely used in the literature; if the phenomenon only appears under gradual sparsification, it becomes a property of the stepwise relaxation rather than of sparsity per se. Similarly, pruning at initialization (SNIP, GraSP) fixes a mask before any training, which could produce a fundamentally different trajectory. The paper provides no justification for the 20% step size and does not argue why gradual pruning should be the relevant regime.

nodes.title: The iterative pruning protocol (20% per step, lottery-ticket rewinding) has not been tested with alternative pruning protocols (one-shot, SNIP, GraSP, varying step fraction)

nodes.content: In the iterative pruning experiments for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 40% symmetric label noise, test accuracy at the Critical Phase sparsity (where the test accuracy is lowest) is measured after the same number of retraining epochs as the dense model (160 epochs total per retraining step). The experiments do not examine whether extending the number of training epochs at Critical Phase sparsities would allow the test accuracy to recover (i.e., whether the observed drop is a transient convergence phenomenon rather than a fundamental overfitting regime). Training accuracy converges to steady state early, but it is not demonstrated that test accuracy has converged by the end of 160 epochs at Critical Phase sparsities. If test accuracy would increase significantly with more epochs, then the claim that moderate sparsity aggravates overfitting would be invalidated—the model is simply undertrained, not overfitting.

metadata.failure_mode: If the test accuracy drop at the Critical Phase disappears with longer training, the conclusion that moderate sparsity aggravates overfitting is false for that setting; the model simply needs more training. This would also affect the four-phase framework (Conclusion 2), because the boundaries would shift with training duration, and the Critical Phase would be recharacterised as a transient finite-epoch effect rather than a fundamental sparsity regime.
metadata.weakness_reason: Training dynamics plots in the paper show train accuracy stabilizing early, but test accuracy per sparsity is not plotted as a function of training epochs at the Critical Phase. In the deep double descent literature, the number of epochs strongly modulates double descent behavior (Nakkiran et al., 2020). It is plausible that moderate sparsities slow optimization, requiring more epochs to reach steady-state generalization. The paper's claim that models "converge to steady states" is based on train accuracy only; test accuracy at critical sparsities might still be improving after the fixed budget of 160 epochs.

nodes.title: Test accuracy drop in Critical Phase may recover with longer training

nodes.content:
For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 under 20% symmetric label noise, the $\ell_2$ learning distance from initialization to learned weights (with pruned weights set to zero) decreases monotonically as sparsity increases from 0% to approximately 90%, showing no peak or plateau near the sparsity range where test accuracy is lowest (the Critical Phase, an intermediate sparsity interval where training accuracy remains high but test accuracy drops). Over the same sparsity range, the test accuracy exhibits a double-descent curve: it drops at the Critical Phase and then rises. Therefore, the learning distance does not match the shape of the test accuracy curve in this case, contradicting the hypothesis that learning distance correlates with sparse double descent (the three-stage non-monotonic dependence of test accuracy on sparsity). The discrepancy is attributed to scale invariance from ReLU activations and batch normalization, but this explanation is not tested.
      Fig. 12 left panel / Fig. 48 left panel

metadata.failure_mode: If learning distance does not track test accuracy on CIFAR-100, the conclusion that "the ℓ2 learning distance often tracks the sparse double descent curve" is false for a major experimental setting. The claim that learning distance "reflect[s] generalization better than flatness in sparse regimes" is also undermined because a metric that fails on a core test case cannot be said to be predictive. The hypothesis would be reduced to an MNIST-specific observation.

refs.text: Fig. 12 left panel / Fig. 48 left panel

metadata.weakness_reason: CIFAR-100 is a central dataset in the paper; its 100-class label-noise setting provides a strong test of the correlation claim. The clear discrepancy between the monotonic distance curve and the U-shaped test accuracy curve shows that the distance measure is not a reliable predictor of generalization in this regime. The proffered explanation—scale invariance—is post hoc and untested (no experiments removing batch normalisation or using a scale-invariant distance). Without a resolution, the hypothesis remains partial and insufficiently validated.

nodes.title: Learning distance fails to show peak for CIFAR-100

nodes.content:
During iterative pruning with magnitude-based scoring for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 containing 40% symmetric label noise, the test accuracy at the epoch that achieves the best performance over the full training trajectory declines from about 50% at 0% sparsity to about 45% at 70% sparsity (the Critical Phase, an intermediate sparsity interval where training accuracy remains high but test accuracy drops), then recovers to about 49% by 90% sparsity (the Sweet Phase, a higher sparsity regime where test accuracy improves substantially). This drop of 5 percentage points is comparable to the drop observed in the final-epoch test accuracy at the same sparsities. Hence the experimental results do not support the claim that the best accuracy shows only a slight drop in the Critical Phase and lacks a well-defined double-descent shape.
      Fig. 11 left panel

metadata.failure_mode: If the best accuracy exhibits a clear double-descent drop, the claim that the best accuracy "may not possess such well-defined trend" and shows only "a slight drop in Critical Phase" is falsified for magnitude pruning. The practical implication—pruning benefits are clearer when considering best accuracy—still holds, but the nuance that the Critical Phase hurts even best accuracy must be acknowledged, reducing the strength of the qualitative description.
metadata.weakness_reason: The discrepancy between the paper's textual description (slight drop, lack of well-defined double descent) and the visual data (clear 5‑point drop) is a factual inaccuracy for the mainline pruning method. While the broader conclusion that pruning can improve peak achievable accuracy at sweet sparsities remains intact, the characterisation of the best-accuracy curve is overstated.

nodes.title: Best test accuracy drops by 5 percentage points in Critical Phase under magnitude pruning

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 40% symmetric label noise, random unstructured pruning (which assigns each weight an independent uniformly drawn random score and prunes those with the lowest scores) produces a test accuracy curve as a function of sparsity that shows the same three-stage non-monotonic pattern as magnitude-based and gradient-based pruning: test accuracy first decreases at moderate sparsities (Critical Phase), then increases at higher sparsities (Sweet Phase), then declines at extreme sparsities (Collapsed Phase). The sparsity ranges for these phases are similar across the three pruning heuristics.

metadata.credit: Without the random-pruning result, one could argue that sparse double descent is an artifact of the specific weight-selection heuristic (magnitude- or gradient-based), perhaps because those heuristics systematically remove parameters that serve as implicit regularizers. Random pruning eliminates this alternative explanation by showing that any sparsity pattern—even a completely unstructured one—leads to the same qualitative behavior. This underwrites the interpretation that the phenomenon is intrinsic to the sparsity level, not to the choice of which weights to remove, thereby strengthening the conclusion's generalizability.

nodes.title: Random pruning reproduces sparse double descent

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 40% symmetric label noise, three different retraining methods produce the characteristic sparse double descent curve: finetuning (continuing from the final trained weights with a fixed small learning rate of 0.001), learning-rate rewinding (continuing from the final weights but reusing the learning rate schedule from the early training phase), and scratch retraining (starting from a fresh random initialization and retraining with the full schedule). In all three cases, the test accuracy first declines at moderate sparsities (Critical Phase), then rises at higher sparsities (Sweet Phase), before finally collapsing at extreme sparsities.

metadata.credit: This result guards against the failure mode that the phenomenon is an artifact of the lottery-ticket rewinding procedure (LTR) used as the default. LTR rewinds to the original initialization, which could impose a favorable inductive bias. By showing the same pattern under finetuning (no rewinding, starts from final weights) and scratch retraining (no reuse of original initialization), the paper demonstrates that the phenomenon is not contingent on rewinding. This underwrites the generalization of the conclusion across retraining protocols and supports the claim that sparsity itself, not the retraining scheme, drives the observed double descent.

nodes.title: Three retraining methods all show the phenomenon

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 40% symmetric label noise at a high sparsity (Sweet Phase), a 1-D linear interpolation between the converged sparse solution (where pruned weights are set to zero) and the re-dense solution (obtained by initializing the recovered pruned weights at zero and retraining the full network with a learning rate of 0.001 for 160 epochs) yields a training loss that monotonically decreases as the interpolation parameter alpha increases from 0 to 1, with the validation accuracy monotonically increasing over the same path.

metadata.credit: This geometric evidence directly refutes the hypothesis that pruning places the model in a flat basin of the dense loss landscape. Without the interpolation, one could argue that the escape observed in re-dense training (Figure 6) is due to optimizer dynamics (e.g., large gradients from zero-initialised recovered weights) rather than the landscape shape. The interpolation shows that even the direct linear path to the re-dense solution has monotonically decreasing loss, conclusively demonstrating that the sparse solution is not a minimizer in the full space. This provides strong evidence that minima flatness (in the dense space) cannot explain sparse double descent.

nodes.title: Linear interpolation shows sparse solutions are not minimizers in full space

nodes.content: The paper's empirical observation that the ℓ2 distance from the original dense initialization to the learned weights (with pruned weights set to zero) peaks near the Critical Phase and then decreases in the Sweet Phase, correlating with improved test accuracy, is consistent with existing theoretical results from Nagarajan & Kolter (2019) and Li et al. (2020b). Specifically, Nagarajan & Kolter derived a generalization bound for deep networks that scales with the ℓ2 distance from initialization, implying that smaller distance leads to better generalization. Li et al. showed that overparameterized neural networks trained with early stopping stay close to initialization and are robust to label noise. Together, these works provide a theoretical basis for why smaller learning distance could reduce memorization of noisy labels.

metadata.credit: Without this consonance with established theory, the learning distance observation would be a purely empirical pattern that could be a spurious correlation (e.g., both distance and generalization are independently correlated with sparsity). The theoretical backing provides a causal pathway—distance bounds capacity, which constrains memorization—converting the observation from a pattern into a candidate mechanism. This underwrites the conclusion that learning distance is a meaningful predictor of sparse double descent, beyond the paper's own experiments.

refs.text: Nagarajan & Kolter, 2019, "Generalization in deep networks: The role of distance from initialization"
Li et al., 2020b, "Gradient descent with early stopping is provably robust to label noise for overparameterized neural networks"

nodes.title: Learning distance hypothesis consistent with prior theory

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with 20% symmetric label noise, the test accuracy of the scratch-reinitialized model (trained from a fresh random initialization at each pruning step) surpasses that of the lottery-ticket model (trained from the original dense initialization using lottery-ticket rewinding) at 90% sparsity: approximately 60% vs. approximately 55%, with standard-deviation error bars over 3 runs not overlapping. The same qualitative advantage of scratch reinitialization holds across noise levels (20%, 40%, 80%) and on CIFAR-100 (as shown in additional figures).

metadata.credit: This specific quantitative comparison with non-overlapping error bars provides concrete evidence that a sparse subnetwork paired with a random initialization can outperform the same mask paired with the original initialization. Without this result, one could maintain that the lottery ticket hypothesis is universally valid and that lottery-ticket rewinding is always optimal. The finding delimits the scope of the lottery ticket hypothesis, showing it fails in certain sparsity regimes under label noise. This underwrites the conclusion that a winning lottery ticket is not guaranteed.

nodes.title: Quantitative comparison shows reinitialization outperforms LTR at certain sparsities

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 40% symmetric label noise, the best test accuracy achieved at any epoch during training increases from the Light Phase to a peak in the early Sweet Phase for all three pruning heuristics: magnitude-based pruning (from approximately 50% to approximately 52%), gradient-based pruning (from approximately 50% to approximately 53%), and random pruning (from approximately 45% to approximately 52%). The improvement is consistent across heuristics, with the Sweet Phase peak surpassing the dense model's best accuracy.

metadata.credit: By showing that the best-test-accuracy improvement from pruning holds across three heuristics, the paper rules out the alternative explanation that the improvement is an artifact of a specific weight-selection strategy. The random-pruning result is especially strong because it uses no selection at all. This consistency underwrites the practical implication: practitioners can expect pruning's benefit for best achievable accuracy even when using simple or random pruning methods, not just carefully designed heuristics.

nodes.title: Best accuracy improvement consistent across three pruning methods

steps.reasoning: Define the classifier function and model sparsity used throughout the experiments as follows: denote the training dataset by $\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, denote model parameters (weights) by $\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ where $d$ is the total number of weights, denote an element-wise binary mask by $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^d$ so that pruned parameters are represented by $\mathbf{w}\odot\mathbf{m}$ where $\odot$ is the element-wise product, and define model sparsity as $1-\sum_{i=1}^d \mathbf{m}_i/d$ (the fraction of removed weights).

Describe the pruning procedure used to produce increasing sparsity: iterative unstructured pruning is applied to individual weights (i.e., global unstructured pruning), pruning removes $20\%$ of weights during each pruning operation in the mainline experiments, and after each pruning the network is retrained using one of several retraining protocols (so sparsity is grown gradually via repeated prune+retrain cycles). This procedural description explains how the authors vary sparsity systematically to measure its effect on test performance.
Han et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019

List the models, datasets, label-noise regimes, pruning heuristics and retraining schemes varied in the empirical study to demonstrate robustness of the observed effect: models include LeNet-300-100, ResNet-18, VGG-16 and ResNet-101; datasets include MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; label-noise regimes include synthetic symmetric noise, asymmetric noise and pairflip noise with noise rate $\epsilon$ set to 20\%, 40\% and 80\%; pruning heuristics include magnitude-based pruning, gradient-based pruning and random pruning; retraining schemes include lottery-ticket rewinding (rewind to an early iteration), finetuning, learning-rate rewinding, and scratch retraining (random reinitialization). These choices are used across the experiments reported in the paper.
Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 20, Fig. 30

Report the core empirical pattern observed when plotting test performance (and train performance) as a function of model sparsity produced by the iterative pruning procedure: as sparsity increases from zero, test performance (measured by test accuracy or test error depending on plot) first degrades (worse than the dense model), then at higher sparsities test performance recovers and improves substantially (often exceeding the earlier degraded region), and finally at extreme sparsities performance collapses as too many useful parameters have been removed. The authors refer to this non-monotonic, three-stage dependence of test performance on sparsity as "sparse double descent."
Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 4

Support the three-stage description with specific empirical visual evidence: (a) Figure 1 (LeNet-300-100 on MNIST and ResNet-18 on CIFAR with 20\% symmetric label noise) shows test accuracy decreasing at moderate sparsities then rising at higher sparsities and finally falling toward extreme sparsities; (b) Figure 2 (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with 40\% symmetric label noise) shows the same three-stage pattern under magnitude-based, gradient-based, and random pruning (i.e., the middle plot demonstrates that even random pruning can produce the first decrease then increase behavior); (c) Figure 4 (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 for $\epsilon=20\%$, $\epsilon=40\%$, $\epsilon=80\%$) shows that the same qualitative three-stage test-accuracy vs sparsity curve occurs across multiple label-noise levels up to 80\%.
Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 4

Document that this sparse double descent phenomenon appears robust across the enumerated experimental choices by referencing the large suite of additional figures spanning architectures, datasets, pruning strategies, retraining methods and noise types: Figures 13–19, 21–29, and 30 in the appendix reproduce the non-monotonic pattern across LeNet-300-100, ResNet-18, VGG-16 and ResNet-101 on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet under magnitude/gradient/random pruning and under symmetric/asymmetric/pairflip noise, and Figures 3 and 26–27 show sparse double descent persists for different retraining schemes (finetuning, learning-rate rewinding, scratch retraining, lottery-ticket rewinding).
Fig. 3, Fig. 13, Fig. 14, Fig. 15, Fig. 16, Fig. 17, Fig. 18, Fig. 19, Fig. 20, Fig. 21, Fig. 22, Fig. 23, Fig. 24, Fig. 25, Fig. 26, Fig. 27, Fig. 28, Fig. 29, Fig. 30

Note control checks and convergence evidence that rule out trivial artifacts: the authors report that models across all sparsities are able to converge to steady states (training curves with respect to epochs are shown in Figures 35 and 36), indicating the observed increases in test accuracy at higher sparsities are not simply due to incomplete optimization at some sparsities but reflect different generalization behavior induced by sparsity changes.
Fig. 35, Fig. 36

Conclude from the experimental breadth and the repeated reproduction across settings that iterative unstructured pruning can produce the described non-monotonic, three-stage dependence of test performance on sparsity (termed "sparse double descent"), and that this phenomenon is observed across multiple network architectures (LeNet-300-100, ResNet-18, VGG-16, ResNet-101), datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet), label-noise regimes (symmetric/asymmetric/pairflip noise with $\epsilon$ up to 80\%), pruning heuristics (magnitude-based, gradient-based, random), and retraining schemes (lottery-ticket rewinding, finetuning, learning-rate rewinding, scratch retraining), supporting the claim that sparse double descent is robust to these experimental choices.
Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4

Start from the empirical discovery of sparse double descent established earlier (conclusion 1) and the repeated plots of train and test accuracy vs sparsity (multiple figures). Use these empirical observations to define contiguous sparsity regimes that summarize recurring qualitative behaviors seen along the sparsity axis.

Define the Light Phase: specify that "Light Phase" corresponds to low sparsity values (i.e., sparsity close to zero) where the pruned network remains sufficiently overparameterized so that it can reach similar training and test accuracy as the original dense model; this behavior is observed in plots where test accuracy near zero sparsity stays high and similar to the dense baseline.
Fig. 5, Fig. 1

Define the Critical Phase: specify that "Critical Phase" is the intermediate sparsity interval around an interpolation threshold (the interpolation threshold concept is borrowed from the literature on double descent) where training accuracy remains high (or does not drop substantially) while test accuracy drops (indicating aggravated overfitting). The paper identifies this phase empirically as the sparsity range where test accuracy first decreases as sparsity grows while training accuracy is preserved.
Fig. 5

Define the Sweet Phase: specify that "Sweet Phase" refers to higher sparsities beyond the Critical Phase where test accuracy improves substantially relative to the Critical Phase, interpreted as reduced overfitting; this is the recovery region in the sparse double descent curve where pruning appears to help generalization.
Fig. 5, Fig. 2

Define the Collapsed Phase: specify that "Collapsed Phase" denotes extreme sparsities where too many parameters have been removed so that both training accuracy and test accuracy drop (the network no longer has enough capacity to fit training data or generalize).
Fig. 5

Provide empirical corroboration that these four contiguous regimes explain observed effects across noise levels: the authors report that increasing the fraction of label noise $\epsilon$ shifts the Critical Phase toward models with larger capacity (equivalently, lower sparsity values) and shifts the Sweet Phase toward higher sparsities (i.e., more pruning is needed to combat heavier label noise), as seen in the experimental plots varying $\epsilon$.
Fig. 4

Summarize the operational criteria used by the authors to distinguish phases in plots: the Light Phase is where pruned networks reach dense-model performance; the Critical Phase is the sparsity interval around the interpolation threshold with preserved training accuracy but decreased test accuracy; the Sweet Phase is the sparsity interval with a pronounced uplift in test accuracy; and the Collapsed Phase is the region where both train and test accuracy fall—these definitions are grounded in the training/test accuracy traces shown in the referenced figures.
Fig. 6

Take as known the empirical discovery of sparse double descent (conclusion 1) and the four-phase characterization of sparsity (conclusion 2); treat those results as established starting points for the present reasoning.

Define the Critical Phase in operational terms for this derivation: it is the sparsity interval around the interpolation threshold where, empirically, training accuracy remains high (i.e., the network still fits training data) while test accuracy drops—this defines the characteristic signature of aggravated overfitting under moderate sparsity.
Fig. 5

Provide empirical evidence that, within the Critical Phase, increasing sparsity can reduce test accuracy while leaving training accuracy nearly unchanged: show training- and test-accuracy traces versus sparsity where the train accuracy curve stays high while the test accuracy curve dips in the intermediate sparsity region — for example, Figures 1, 2 and the detailed plots in the appendix (Figures 13–29) display this pattern across architectures and datasets, and Figures 35–36 show per-epoch training dynamics confirming that models at these intermediate sparsities still reach high training accuracy while test accuracy is reduced.
Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 35, Fig. 36

Note that this deterioration (worse test accuracy with preserved train accuracy) occurs under different pruning rules (magnitude-based, gradient-based, random pruning): the right panels of Figure 2 and the appendix figures for random pruning reproduce the Critical Phase behavior, indicating the phenomenon is not specific to a particular pruning heuristic but can also appear under random pruning.
Fig. 2, Fig. 13, Fig. 16

Note that this deterioration also occurs under different retraining methods (lottery-ticket rewinding, finetuning, learning-rate rewinding, scratch retraining): Figure 3 and appendix figures for different retraining protocols show that the Critical Phase signature — preserved training accuracy coupled with decreased test accuracy — remains present across retraining variants, indicating the Critical Phase is not an artifact of a single retraining protocol.
Fig. 3, Fig. 15, Fig. 19

Synthesize these empirical points to conclude that moderate sparsity (the Critical Phase) can aggravate overfitting: within the Critical Phase, pruning can increase the generalization gap (test accuracy drops while train accuracy is preserved), and this effect occurs across pruning rules and retraining methods, demonstrating the Critical Phase is a robust empirical phenomenon rather than an experimental artifact tied to one heuristic.
Fig. 32

State the experimental protocol used to probe whether pruning leads to flat minima: apply "re-dense training" where, after training a sparse network to convergence, the pruned weights are recovered, initialized to zero, and the full dense network (including recovered weights) is retrained for additional epochs using a small learning rate equal to the last sparse-training learning rate; this procedure is used to test whether the sparse solution lies in a flat basin of the dense loss landscape (if stuck in a flat basin, re-dense training with a small learning rate would be expected to remain near the sparse solution).
Han et al., 2017
Fig. 6

Describe the observed re-dense training dynamics: when pruned weights are reintroduced (initialized to zero) and the dense network is retrained with a small learning rate, the optimizer often departs from the sparse solution and moves to different dense minima that overfit (i.e., training accuracy increases while test accuracy degrades), indicating instability of the sparse solutions inside the dense parameter space.
Fig. 6, Fig. 37, Fig. 38, Fig. 39

Provide evidence from linear-interpolation visualizations of loss along the line segment connecting sparse solution $\mathbf{w}_s$ and re-dense solution $\mathbf{w}_r$: compute $\mathbf{w}(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{w}_s+\alpha\mathbf{w}_r$ for $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and measure loss/accuracy along this path; plots reveal a monotonically decreasing loss from sparse to re-dense points in some cases, which implies that the sparse solution is not a local minimizer of the dense loss and that a descent path exists leading away from the sparse point toward sharper, lower-loss dense minima.
Fig. 7, Fig. 40, Fig. 41, Fig. 42

Report curvature/sharpness evidence from 1-D loss visualizations using filter-wise normalization: the 1-D visualizations of loss around re-dense minima show that the final re-dense solutions are often sharper (higher curvature) than the original dense models, and that sparser original pruned networks tend to converge to sharper re-dense minima after re-dense training, which contradicts the hypothesis that pruning promotes flatter minima that explain improved generalization.
Fig. 8, Fig. 43

Conclude that minima flatness cannot account for the observed sparse double descent in the reported cases because (a) sparse solutions are not stable under re-dense training even with small learning rates, (b) there exist monotonically descending loss paths from sparse to re-dense solutions indicating the sparse solutions are not dense minima, and (c) re-dense solutions can be sharper and yet overfit—therefore the conjecture that pruning promotes flat minima which in turn explain improved generalization does not hold for these empirical observations.
Fig. 6, Fig. 7, Fig. 8

Start from the empirical refutation of minima-flatness as a universal explanation (conclusion 4) and from the observed sparse double descent phenomenon (conclusion 1); the authors leverage these motivations to propose and test an alternate measure, the $\ell_2$ learning distance.

Define the $\ell_2$ learning distance precisely and unambiguously: denote the original dense model initialization by $\mathbf{w}_{init}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, denote the learned weights after the $i$-th pruning and retraining by $\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with pruned entries set to zero, and define the learning distance $D(\mathbf{w}_{init},\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i) = \|\mathbf{w}_{init}-\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i\|_2$ (the Euclidean norm in $\mathbb{R}^d$).

Provide empirical observations linking the learning distance curve to the sparse double descent test-accuracy curve: when plotting $D$ against model sparsity alongside test accuracy vs sparsity, the authors observe that (a) in the Critical Phase the learning distance often attains higher values (models move further from initialization) and those models show worse test performance, (b) in the Sweet Phase the learning distance tends to be smaller (models stay closer to initialization) and test performance improves, and (c) the turning point of test accuracy from decreasing to increasing often coincides with a peak in learning distance — these empirical correspondences are shown in figures for MNIST and CIFAR variants.
Fig. 9, Fig. 44, Fig. 46, Fig. 48

Document that the empirical correlations hold across datasets and retraining protocols to a substantial extent: the paper reports learning-distance vs sparsity and test-accuracy vs sparsity plots for LeNet-300-100 on MNIST under several noise rates and retraining protocols (Figures 9, 44, 45), and for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under multiple retraining methods (Figures 46–49), showing similar qualitative linkage between $D$ and test performance across these settings.
Fig. 44, Fig. 45, Fig. 46, Fig. 47, Fig. 48, Fig. 49

Acknowledge empirical caveats and factors that can weaken the direct correspondence: the authors note that on some CIFAR experiments the Critical Phase test accuracy is lower than dense while the critical learning distance is not higher than the dense case, and they attribute part of this discrepancy to ReLU scale invariance and batch-normalization reparameterizations (which can alter $\ell_2$ distances without changing function represented), thereby explaining why learning distance is not a perfect predictor in all cases.
Nagarajan & Kolter (2019)

Conclude that the $\ell_2$ learning distance $D(\mathbf{w}_{init},\mathbf{w}_{learned}^i)$ empirically correlates with sparse double descent behavior and can, in the studied sparse regimes, reflect generalization trends better than minima flatness; thus the learning-distance hypothesis is proposed as a useful predictor of when pruning will aggravate or relieve overfitting, while the authors note theoretical justification remains an open question.
Fig. 9, Fig. 12

Take as known the empirical discovery that sparse double descent occurs across many settings (conclusion 1); use that empirical context to compare retraining protocols that keep the original initialization (lottery-ticket rewinding) versus those that reinitialize the pruned subnetwork (scratch retraining).

Define the retraining protocols compared: lottery-ticket rewinding (rewind parameters and learning rate to an early training iteration and retrain the pruned network from that near-initialization point) versus scratch retraining (rewind the learning-rate schedule but use a fresh random reinitialization of the pruned network and retrain for full epochs). These definitions follow the retraining taxonomy used in the experiments.
Frankle & Carbin (2019)

Present empirical comparisons showing that random reinitialization can outperform rewinding at some sparsities and data/noise settings: Figure 10 (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with $\epsilon=20\%$) shows cases where the test accuracy of the scratch (reinitialized) pruned models exceeds that of the lottery-ticket (rewound) counterparts at the same sparsity, and Figures 33 and 34 in the appendix provide further plots over $\epsilon=20\%$, $\epsilon=40\%$, and $\epsilon=80\%$ documenting the same behavior across noise levels and datasets.
Fig. 10, Fig. 33, Fig. 34

Explain the practical implication: because the same sparse mask (i.e., the same subnetwork structure) can yield better test accuracy when trained from a fresh random initialization than when retrained from its original dense initialization in some sparsity regimes (notably under label noise and within sparse double descent settings), a "winning lottery ticket" (a subnetwork that performs well when trained from the original initialization) is not guaranteed to outperform reinitialized training across all sparsities and settings.

Conclude that empirical evidence demonstrates that retraining a pruned subnetwork from random scratch can sometimes yield higher test accuracy than retraining from the original initialization (lottery-ticket rewinding), so a winning ticket is not guaranteed to win at all sparsities or noise regimes exhibiting sparse double descent.

Use the empirical sparse double descent results (conclusion 1) and training-epoch-dependent behavior noted in the literature as context: deep double descent depends on training epochs as well as model capacity, suggesting that evaluating the best test accuracy attained across training (rather than only final-epoch accuracy) can reveal different effects of pruning on attainable performance.
Nakkiran et al., 2020

Define "best test accuracy" as the maximum test accuracy achieved at any epoch during training (as distinct from final-epoch test accuracy), and state that the authors plot both training accuracy and best test accuracy versus sparsity to investigate how pruning affects the best-achievable generalization during training.

Present empirical evidence that pruning can improve the best-achievable test accuracy before eventual collapse at extreme sparsities: Figure 11 shows that, for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 with $\epsilon=40\%$ across three pruning strategies, the best test accuracy (the maximum over epochs) tends to increase from the Light Phase into the early Sweet Phase (i.e., peak best-test moves upward with moderate-to-high sparsity) before dropping at extreme sparsities in the Collapsed Phase—this is contrasted with the last-epoch test accuracy which exhibits sparse double descent.
Fig. 11

Explain the authors' interpretation: the increase in best test accuracy with some pruning is plausibly due to pruning-induced implicit regularization that affects training dynamics (for example, by limiting memorization of noisy labels and shifting the training trajectory to regions where early stopping yields better validation performance), so pruning can enlarge the attainable peak validation performance even though final-epoch accuracy displays sparse double descent.

Conclude that while final-epoch test accuracy shows sparse double descent, pruning often increases the peak test performance attained during training from the Light Phase into early Sweet Phase before eventual collapse at extreme sparsities, meaning pruning can improve the best-achievable test accuracy across epochs in many experimental settings.

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly acknowledges several unresolved scientific issues that remain after its empirical findings: (1) a rigorous theoretical account proving or falsifying the proposed learning-distance hypothesis for sparse neural networks is lacking — in particular, a principled derivation that links $\ell_2$ distance-from-initialization to memorization propensity and to the three-phase sparse double descent curve; (2) the precise role of scale invariances (e.g., ReLU and batch normalization reparametrizations) in modulating measured learning distance and its predictive power is not resolved and can distort $\ell_2$-based diagnostics; (3) the mechanisms that determine the location and width of the Critical Phase and Sweet Phase as functions of dataset difficulty, label-noise rate, architecture, and training schedule are not characterized; (4) the reasons why certain retraining strategies (e.g., rewinding vs. scratch reinitialization) outperform others at particular sparsities remain unexplained in theory; and (5) more generally, a unified theoretical framework connecting sparse-induced reshaping of the loss landscape (including creation of spurious minima/valleys), optimization dynamics under sparsity constraints, and generalization in noisy-label regimes is left open for future work.
